passage:
I'm Aadhya, and I sit behind Yash in class. His father died in March. Yesterday at the school prayer Yash stood at the back with his arms folded and didn't sing. In the corridor afterwards he said, loudly, "What kind of god takes someone like that?" Then he looked around and said sorry.
Our teacher told him, "You don't need to apologise for that." The teacher said he could be angry, and that some people find comfort in prayer and some in other people, and neither is wrong.
At lunch his uncle, who prays every morning, sat next to him and they ate without talking. I can't say what Yash truly believes. He might be angry, or just tired. But he ate the whole roti.

qa.q: Where did Yash stand during the school prayer?
qa.a: He stood at the back with his arms folded.

qa.q: What might Yash be feeling, judging from what Aadhya saw?
qa.a: He may be angry at God and perhaps tired as well: he asked 'What kind of god takes someone like that?', though Aadhya admits she can't be sure.

qa.q: How could a friend support Yash?
qa.a: A friend can let him voice his anger without judging, sit with him as his uncle did, and accept that he may find comfort in faith or in people.

qa.q: How might Yash's uncle see the moment at lunch?
qa.a: The uncle may see it as a time simply to be there, sitting and eating without talking, even though he himself finds comfort in prayer.

grounding: An observer describes a bereaved classmate's anger at God, voiced aloud, and shows that faith and people are both acceptable comforts.

passage: Gurleen, can I just say this out loud once without you fixing it? I'm Tushar, and I'm angry at God. There. Maa kept every fast, went to the temple every Tuesday, prayed for everyone in the building. And she still got sick, and she still died in March. So where was He? At the thirteenth-day puja I couldn't even fold my hands. Mausi said I'd feel better if I prayed. I didn't. I went up to the terrace and shouted at the sky instead, like an idiot. You know what, though? After shouting, I could breathe. The old pandit ji found me there later. He didn't scold. He said even saints argued with God, and sometimes anger is a kind of prayer. I don't know if I believe that. Maybe I'll find my way back to the temple, maybe not. Right now what helps is you, cricket on Sundays, and Maa's recipe book. That's allowed, right?

qa.q: Where did Tushar go instead of praying?
qa.a: Up to the terrace, to shout at the sky.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling at the thirteenth-day puja?
qa.a: Tushar felt angry and betrayed by God, unable even to fold hands in prayer.

qa.q: What helps Tushar right now, and why is that okay?
qa.a: Gurleen, Sunday cricket and Maa's recipe book; comfort from people is as valid as comfort from faith.

qa.q: How does the old pandit ji see Tushar's anger?
qa.a: He doesn't scold; he sees anger as part of grief, even a kind of prayer.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen angry with God after a parent's death, voicing it and finding comfort in people while faith stays open.

passage: The week of the funeral. Santosh refused to go into the church. His cousin Pankaj had been nineteen, the one who taught him to ride a bike, and a fever had taken him in four days. 'If God is good, why Pankaj?' Santosh shouted at his mother in the parking lot, then felt terrible for shouting. Three weeks later. Father Thomas found him sitting on the church steps after youth group, kicking gravel. 'You can be angry with God here, you know. He can take it.' Santosh said nothing, but he stayed, and they talked about Pankaj until the lights went off. Two months later. On Pankaj's birthday, Santosh lit a candle in the side chapel. He still had questions no one could answer. But sitting in the quiet, saying Pankaj's name, gave him a kind of peace he hadn't found anywhere else.

qa.q: What did Santosh do on Pankaj's birthday?
qa.a: He lit a candle in the side chapel.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling in the parking lot the week of the funeral?
qa.a: He felt furious at God for taking Pankaj, then guilty for shouting at his mother.

qa.q: What helped Santosh voice his anger safely?
qa.a: Talking with Father Thomas on the church steps, where he was told he could be angry with God there.

qa.q: How does Father Thomas see Santosh's anger?
qa.a: He sees it as something God can take and welcomes it rather than scolding.

grounding: Shows a teen angry with God after a cousin's death, voicing it and slowly finding comfort in faith over weeks.
